keyVerseText: And he answered and told them, Elias verily cometh first, and restoreth all things; and how it is written of the Son of man, that he must suffer many things, and be set at nought.
rootMeaning: The Greek verb ἐξουδενόω (exoudenóō) derives from the preposition ἐκ (ek), meaning 'out of' or 'from,' combined with a derivative of οὐδείς (oudeis), meaning 'no one' or 'nothing.' This etymology suggests a literal sense of 'to make out of nothing' or 'to reduce to nothing,' which enriches the common English gloss 'to set at nought' by emphasizing the act of utterly disregarding or despising something as if it were nothing at all.
usageInScripture: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, specifically in Mark 9:12, where it is translated as 'be set at nought.' Its singular occurrence highlights a focused use that consistently conveys the idea of despising or treating something as worthless. This consistency in translation underscores the verb’s strong connotation of contempt or rejection, rather than a mild disregard.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding ἐξουδενόω helps believers grasp the depth of contempt that can be directed toward Christ and His mission, as well as the human tendency to reject divine truth. Theologically, it reveals the stark reality of how the Son of Man’s sufferings were not merely physical but involved being utterly despised and disregarded by many. Recognizing this verb’s force invites a humble response of reverence and faith, acknowledging Christ’s willingness to endure such rejection for our salvation. It also challenges believers to avoid the same attitude of despising what God values.
keyVerseReflection: In Mark 9:12, Jesus explains that the Son of Man 'must suffer many things, and be set at nought,' using ἐξουδενόω to convey the profound rejection He would face. This word highlights not only the suffering but the dishonor and contempt involved in His passion. It deepens our understanding of the cost of redemption, reminding us that Christ endured being treated as worthless to restore all things, fulfilling the prophecy about Elijah’s coming and the restoration of all.
